QUOTED QUESTION: Why is it a bad argument to demand that we must be able to name new knowledge now in order for it to be considered real?
QUOTED SOURCE: 2023-02-11_Naval interview - Knowledge Creation and The Human Race Part 1_qafixed.md
QUOTED TIMESTAMP: [13:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YyxepLfH1ZU&t=829)
QUOTED ANSWER: It does _seem like a catch-22 to demand that we must be able to name new knowledge now in order for it to be considered real_, and it's a bad argument. I don't want to claim that the knowledge will be created. We're fallible. We may not create it. We may destroy ourselves. We may miss the solution that's right under our nose so that when the Snailiens come from another galaxy and look at us, they'll say, "How can it possibly be that they failed to do so-and-so when it was right in front of them?" That could happen. I can't prove or argue that it won't happen. What I always do argue, though, is that we have what it takes. We have everything that it takes to achieve that. If we don't, it'll be because of bad choices we have made, not because of constraints imposed on us by the planet or the solar system. *IN-LINE: It will be by anti-rational memes that restrict the creation of knowledge and the growth of knowledge.* Maybe, or maybe it'll be by well-intentioned errors, which nobody could see why they were errors. It doesn't take malevolence to make mistakes. Mistakes are the normal condition of humans. All we can do is try to find them, and maybe not destroying the means of correcting errors is the heart of morality, because if there is no way of correcting errors, then sooner or later one of those will get us.

QUOTED QUESTION: Why is denying AGI personhood equivalent to dualism and a belief in the supernatural?
QUOTED SOURCE: 2023-12-19_Steven Pinker 1 on Joe Walker Podcast - on AGI Doom and Enemies of Civilization_qafixed.md
QUOTED TIMESTAMP: [32:57](https://youtu.be/3Ho-vJZsMgk&t=1977)
QUOTED ANSWER: _Regarding the view that different substrates running arbitrarily similar computations can nonetheless have significantly different emergent properties, i.e the view that a program of the human mind cannot run on another substrate, i.e. the denial of substrate independence of universal computation_, well, you can be a dualist. You can say that there is mind in addition to all the physical stuff. But if you want to be a physicalist, which I do, then... There's this thought experiment where you remove one neuron at a time and replace it by a silicon chip, and you wouldn't notice. *IN-LINE: Well, that's the question. Would you notice? How do you... Why are you so...* Well, if you would notice, then if you claimed...  *IN-LINE: Sorry, let me just change that. An external observer wouldn't notice. How do we know that from the point of view of the brain being replaced, every neuron by a chip, that it's like falling asleep, that when it's done and every last neuron is replaced by a chip, you're dead subjectively, even though your body is still making noise and doing goal-directed things.* Yes, so that means that when your subjectivity is running, there is something happening in addition to the computation, and that's dualism. *IN-LINE: Well, again, I don't have an opinion one way or another, which is exactly my point. I don't think it's a decidable problem. But it could be that that extra something is not a ghostly substance, some sort of Cartesian "res cogitans," separate from the mechanism of the brain. But it could be that the stuff that the brain is made of is responsible for that extra ingredient of subjective experience as opposed to intelligent behavior. At least I suspect people's intuitions would be very... Unless you deliberately program a system to target our emotions, I'm not sure that people would grant subjectivity to an intelligent system.* Actually, people have already granted subjectivity to ChatGPT, so that's already happened. *IN-LINE: But is anyone particularly concerned if you pull a plug on ChatGPT and ready to prosecute someone for murder?* Yes, I mean, I've forgotten details, but just a few weeks ago, one of the employees there declared that the system was sentient. *IN-LINE: That was Blake, Blake Lemoine, a couple of years ago. He was ironically fired for saying that. This is LaMDA, a different large language model.* Oh, right. Okay, so I've got all the details wrong. *IN-LINE: Yeah. He did say it, but his employer disagreed, and I'm not convinced. When I shut down ChatGPT, the version running on my computer, I don't think I've committed murder, and I don't think anyone else would think it.* I don't either, but I don't think it's creative. *IN-LINE: It's pretty creative. In fact, I saw on your website that you reproduced a poem that it's, on electrons. I thought that was pretty creative. So I certainly granted creativity. I'm not ready to grant it subjectivity.* Well, this is a matter of how we use words. I mean, even a calculator can produce a number that's never been seen before. Because you know numbers are exponentially, range over exponentially large range. *IN-LINE: I think it's more than words, though. I mean, it actually is much more than words. So for example, if someone permanently disabled a human, namely kill them, I would be outraged. I want that person punished. __If someone were to dismantle a human-like robot, it'd be awful, it might be a waste, but I'm not going to try that person for murder. I'm not going to lose any sleep over it. There is a difference in intuition. Maybe I'm mistaken. Maybe I'm as callous as the people who didn't grant personhood to slaves in the 18th and 19th centuries, but I don't think so. And although, again, I think we have no way of knowing, I think we're going to be having the same debate 100 years from now.* Yeah, maybe one of the AGIs will be participating in the debate by then.

Nominalism is a philosophical view that deals with the nature of universals and abstract concepts. According to nominalism, universals—things like "beauty," "redness," or "humanity" that could be said to exist in multiple instances—do not have an independent existence outside of the objects that instantiate them. In other words, nominalists argue that universals are merely names or labels we use to describe particular objects or sets of objects, rather than real entities with their own existence.

Nominalism stands in contrast to realism, which posits that universals have an existence independent of the particular things that exhibit them. For example, a realist might argue that the concept of "redness" exists in a real, abstract form beyond any particular red object.

Nominalism plays a significant role in various philosophical debates, including those about language, metaphysics, and epistemology, as it challenges the nature of reality and the way we categorize and understand the world.
